name: Smith River
agency: Montana FWP / Lewis & Clark National Forest

camps.desc: A very nice sandbar beach camp. A single-party site.

camps.name: Rattlesnake

rapids.name: Mile 47 Class II
rapids.desc: One section of Class II water, which Montana FWP lists near the end of the float. Riverbrain describes the Smith as technical Class I overall, with Givens Gulch as the one technical Class II.

rapids.name: Mile 49 Class II
rapids.desc: Several short Class II sections, per Montana FWP. Mostly wave trains. Expect the current to push you to the outside of the turns toward the walls.

items.d: Introduced. The river holds large populations of wild browns, which generally outnumber the rainbows.
Wild rainbows share the river with the browns. Rises to hatches in the cool of morning and evening.
Montana's native trout and state fish. A remnant population survives in Tenderfoot Creek.
A silvery native with a small mouth, found in the runs and deeper pools. Rises to hatches and often bites a nymph.
A bottom-feeding native that sweeps rocky riffles for insects.

indigenous: Many nations have used the Smith River corridor for thousands of years, including the Salish, Kootenai, Blackfeet, Crow, Shoshone and Gros Ventre. The canyon was a travel route, a hunting ground and a place to camp long before it was a float trip.
More than 70 pictograph and rock-art sites have been recorded along the float. Look and photograph, but never touch, trace or chalk the panels, and do not move anything at the sites.
history: On July 15, 1805, the Corps of Discovery reached the mouth of this river on the Missouri. Meriwether Lewis described a beautiful river about 80 yards wide and named it Smith’s River for Robert Smith, the Secretary of the Navy.

The army set up Camp Baker in 1869 to guard the freight route from Fort Benton and the nearby mining camps. It was renamed Fort Logan in 1877 for Captain William Logan, killed at the Battle of the Big Hole, abandoned in 1880 and sold at auction in 1881. The blockhouse is what remains.

Use of the river grew sharply in the 1960s and brought safety problems and conflict with private landowners along the banks. The corridor is now managed by the state as a recreational waterway, with permits, designated boat camps and a lottery.
geology: The canyon walls are mostly Madison Limestone, laid down in warm shallow seas during the Mississippian, about 359 to 326 million years ago. Folding has tilted the beds into long gray palisades, and limestone walls rise about 300 feet from the water in places. Caves have been reported high on the cliffs, as they are wherever water has dissolved the Madison.
flows: The Smith is free-flowing through the float, fed by snowmelt and tributaries such as Tenderfoot Creek. A good year gives a pleasant 3 to 4 day float; a dry year can mean dragging boats by midsummer. Recommended flow guidance: 150 cfs canoes and kayaks, 250 rafts, 350 drift boats.

rules.d: Montana FWP's usual guidance is about 350 cfs for drift boats, 250 cfs for rafts and 150 cfs for canoes and kayaks. Below that the float gets scrapey, and in low years it can be nearly impossible.

Peak season is generally mid-May to mid-July, and most floats run between mid-April and mid-July. In a dry year the river can drop too low to float comfortably by midsummer; some years are boatable into September.
Watch the USGS gauges Smith River near Fort Logan (06076690) and Smith River below Eagle Creek near Fort Logan (06077200), and check the FWP river updates before you launch.

The river is mostly Class I with a few Class II sections, reported near miles 47 and 49. Givens Gulch is the technical one: scout it from river left above the drop, and expect the current to push you to the outside of the turn against the wall.
There are no services, potable water, trash facilities or cell service along the 59 miles. Carry everything you need and a way to call for help.
Treat or filter all drinking water.
Low midsummer water warms enough to stress trout. In hot weather keep fish wet and release them quickly.
Camp only at the designated boat camps. Sites are signed and marked on the FWP maps given out at Camp Baker.
FWP requires human waste to be carried out in an approved portable toilet system. Check the current floater packet for the exact rules.
Rattlesnake (mile 47.4) holds the last boat camps; Eden Bridge is about 11.5 miles below it.

landmarks.name: Camp Baker
landmarks.desc: The put-in, named for the army post set up here in 1869 (renamed Fort Logan in 1877, abandoned 1880). The blockhouse survives and is on the National Register of Historic Places. Highway 89 to Highway 360 (Fort Logan Road) reaches it.

landmarks.name: Tenderfoot Creek
landmarks.desc: Joins the Smith near here (reported near mile 16) and adds noticeable volume to the river. Remnant westslope cutthroat trout still live in the creek.

landmarks.name: Eden Bridge
landmarks.desc: The take-out: the first bridge you meet on the run. By road it is reached from Cascade on Hound Creek Road.

notes.camp: *Camping is at designated boat camps only. This list is partial: Montana FWP lists about 27 named camps and over 50 sites, and several camps are split into upper, middle and lower sites that each hold one party. Use the map and mileage sheet you get at Camp Baker for the full set.

apply.label: Apply on the FWP licensing site

items.d: Use the Montana FWP online licensing service during the application window. You can list several launch dates.
FWP emails winners. Unsuccessful applicants are not notified; results are also posted in your myfwp account.
Winners are called about two days before launch to register the party, declare boat camps and pay float fees. Rangers assign a one-hour launch window.
Every group attends a mandatory safety and orientation talk at Camp Baker on launch day.

From early March, call the Smith River reservation line (406-454-5861, weekdays 8 a.m. to noon Mountain) to pick up cancelled dates or cancel yours. The page gives two different start dates for the line, so confirm.
January 1 to February 15. The drawing is held February 18 (2026 cycle; confirm the next dates).
A separate drawing: applications through March 15, drawn March 16. The winner may launch any date that season.
A permit is required year-round. Most floats run mid-April to mid-July, with some in September and October. From May 15 to July 15 you may camp a maximum of four nights.
A small non-refundable fee per application ($15 in most FWP sources; one 2026 guide says about $10). Confirm on the licensing site.
One point per year may be bought: $5 for residents, $125 for nonresidents. Points build until you draw, then reset.
$5 each; buy as many as you like.
Per-person fees are set in the Smith River biennial rule and paid at phone registration.
Up to 15 people on one permit.
The permit covers the 59-mile float from Camp Baker to Eden Bridge with camping at designated boat camps only.
Motorized boats are not allowed.
Reported cap of nine float parties per day at Camp Baker.

stats.season: Mid-April to early July, with some floating in September. Permits are drawn each February.

flow.note: FWP’s guidance is 150 cfs for canoes and kayaks, 250 for rafts and 350 for drift boats. It does not close the river for low flow, but below these levels floating gets harder and in a very dry summer is discouraged.
